Read: July 2023

Like the last one, I spotted this at a Sisyphe bookstore (a Chinese bookstore chain) and then bought it on JD.com. Only I bought the wrong edition: a teaching edition, rather like a school Chinese textbook. Key passages highlighted throughout, the meaning of this or that sentence analyzed, an illustration every few pages. By far the most frequent analysis: “This reflects the numbness, callousness and feudal ignorance of people at the time.” In an instant I was dragged back to the Chinese lessons of my nine years of compulsory schooling. Having just finished Cho-yun Hsu’s China: A New Cultural History, I couldn’t help asking: how is education today any different from the Ming dynasty, several hundred years ago?

Numb and callous, feudal and ignorant. As an overall verdict, it is fair enough.

The book’s portrait of the Northeast is almost too accurate: the desolation of the frozen land, the bustle of market days and temple fairs, the huge pit in the dirt road and the horse carts that fall into it, the mumbo jumbo of the shamans’ trance dances, the neighbors both warm and indifferent. It is exactly my childhood memory of my hometown. The irony is that nearly a century later, the Northeast is still like this. True, you no longer see the inhuman ignorance of tormenting a young child bride to death, but there is no shortage of ignorance in other forms.

Finishing the book stirred an urge in me to write my own life story. I grew up in a tiny county town in the Northeast, the kind people call “eighteenth-tier.” Before I was eighteen I had never left the province, and I went to university in the province too. Then ten years abroad. Every time I go back to China and then return to Europe, I feel torn in two. The people on each side live in two different worlds. Their lives may never cross, and they couldn’t begin to imagine each other’s lives. Yet both are real, earnestly living their lives, good or bad, six time zones apart, watching the same sun rise and the same moon set. Over there, an auntie finishes her pickled-cabbage dumplings, shovels a scoop of coal into the stove and plays cards with the neighbors, cracking sunflower seeds; over here, an old man finishes his sandwich, tosses two logs on the fire, and picks up a pen and the newspaper to do the sudoku.

I’m about to go home for Chinese New Year, and this time I want to make a point of collecting pictures and sound recordings, and of jotting down whatever fragments of memory get stirred up and whatever I’m thinking in the moment. I haven’t been home for New Year in five years. How much will have changed since five years ago? And how much has changed since the Hulan of the early twentieth century that Xiao Hong wrote about?
